title: Desire and Petition
english: He calls the one possessing it by the name of possession. And I say indeed also concerning the one possessing love that it benefits. And it benefits by that benefit which love provides. If therefore I say that the holy one says this, such as the hymnodist, not separating the Holy Spirit from the one possessing it, nor do I say that the one possessing it says these things apart from the Holy Spirit. If then 'David in the Holy Spirit calls him Lord' (Ps 37:4), so also it is as a partaking, not being severed from the partaker, just as knowledge is not without the knower.

And 'he will rejoice exceedingly in your salvation' (Ps 103:5). The king, just as he is gladdened by power, so also rejoices exceedingly over salvation. And salvation and power are the same, being understood according to one or another conception. Power is that which sustains all things and leads all things thus as it thinks. So also it is salvation; for what he does, he does for the sake of salvation—what he does in men, he does for the sake of the salvation of men.

You gave him the desire of his soul. You know that the word 'himself' denotes authority, not merely the things adjacent. The desire of the soul is bad when, assuming a bad soul, one says 'soul'. But when I say that the soul itself has desire, I speak of its essential desire. The one using desire in this way sees nothing of the bad things, but of the good things; for he received the desiring faculty and the desire, so that he might pursue the beautiful things, so that he might enjoy the profitable things. If, therefore, it happens that he is a lover of silver of wealth, he did not receive the desire of his own soul, but the desire of the lover of silver. Great, therefore, is the happening of the desire of the soul, without adding 'the bad' to it. Indeed, in another psalm he also says: 'the one filling your desire with good things' (Ps 144:11). He speaks to the soul. It has been said to us many times in other places that adjacent words do not make an antithesis. If I say, 'the desire of the soul is good,' and again I say, 'the desire of the righteous is good,' the adjacent words do not make an antithesis. But if I say, 'the desire that is shameful, the desire that is evil, the desire of the unrighteous,' an antithesis is made. That desire is not simply of the soul, but of such a soul. Therefore, the adjacent words sometimes agree, and sometimes they contend and make an antithesis. Thus indeed it is said: 'every desire of a righteous man is good.'

There is no distinction between the desire of a righteous soul and the desire of a soul without addition. And he did not withhold the will of their lips, and this appears even regarding the sensible. If I say now: 'so much as a father desires his children to live well', because I have made a memory of a father, I want them to live well. But if I say: 'an evil father wants his children to do such things', I have removed paternal compassion. 'With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you' (Luke 22:15). And the 'with desire' and 'I have desired' is in such a way as: 'rightly I pursued the righteous', the worthy of being desired. And there is sometimes to desire and also the unworthy of being desired, as it says: 'passion, an evil desire'. An evil desire is not a thing to be desired, just as a pseudo-good is not called heretical, even if some call it so.

3 And he did not withhold his lips' petition from him. If the word is about [the one] from Mary, it is clear that he brings a petition for those for whom he has come to save. You have indeed: 'wherefore also he is able to save to the perfection, always living to intercede for them'. 6 He always lives in interceding. And take 'always' thus: as much as they need, entreating and mediating. 'And if anyone sins, we have a counselor toward the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous' (1 John 2:1). And since the others also run to the teacher with this haste, they also want to intercede for those for whom they were entrusted, not setting their own prior intercession, but following the justification of the one calling them to imitation. According to all the rewards of the king, it is necessary to be careful not to be deprived of his petition. For example, when we speak about the one ruling sensorially, saying that the petition of his lips was not withheld, but it happened in the outcome, we signify his praise. Even if we speak about the saints—for they too are called kings—and there is great praise for them, it is when their petition is well-received. For 'the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears to their petition' (Psalm 34:15), and: 'he hearkens to the prayers of the righteous' (Psalm 34:17).

3 Dipsalmos. 10 The 'dipsalmos' is found nowhere, neither in the Hebrew scriptures, especially in the Psalms. But this also lies in the song of Habakkuk. Those knowing the dialect are able to say what it means.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Precious Stones of Virtue
english: However, we speak of what has come to us. Those who say that it signifies a change of face are lying; for we have found changes of faces in the psalms even without the diapsalma. Again, they say that the diapsalma signifies a certain interval—for example, saying 'he ceased and at another time he began'—and this diapsalma signifies a chronological interval. But we cannot say this; for it is not laid down that he spoke these verses of the psalm after another time.

But those who have conversed with the Hebrew readings say that this is a musical rhythm, just as they say rhythms and melodies in musical matters. Therefore, these things are not for us to know, but for those who have conversed with the dialect. In every dialect, indeed, it is possible to be appropriate to music. Nor is there music or a rhythm of sounds when they are arranged unharmoniously. Sometimes I think I know letters and to comment on readings. And if we see something in a garden, which is named by a farmer because we do not know it, we learn from him, and not already, not devaluing learning, we remain uneducated from this. So, even if we do not know the Hebrew dialect, we have heard that it signifies a musical rhythm according to the Hebrew dialect.

'For you have preceded him in blessings of goodness' (Psalm 21:3). God has preceded the king in all interpretations in blessings of goodness. The 'you have preceded in blessings' is equal to: 'While you are still speaking I will say: behold, I am here' (Psalm 40:2). For example, suppose a certain prayer is being sent up concerning living well, concerning having virtue; it says: 'while you are still speaking,' not yet having fulfilled the word of the prayer, because of the giving, I say I am present.

The 'of goodness' we take here as 'of kindness'; for often we take the 'good' as if toward slander: 'evil characters make the conversations bad,' instead of the pleasant, the kind. And the pleasant itself is taken even regarding praise, when someone has a good character, and regarding the pleasant. Likewise also the innocent: 'for through the good-speaking they deceive the hearts of the innocent.' And also: 'the innocent believes every word.' 'You have set upon his head a crown of precious stone.' If this is said concerning the Lord's man, this crown is that which is placed upon the head...

A crown is woven from his precious stones, that is, from virtues or those possessing virtues. Within the weaving of this crown lie those stones being built up with gold and silver upon the foundation, Christ. It is clear, however, that neither gold, nor silver, nor the stones are taken according to physical sense.

Even regarding each king, such as Abraham was, or as the other saints are, we say this: just as the ruler of Tyre, when he lived well, was placed among the Cherubim in the holy mountain of God, when it was a 'seal of likeness' and a 'crown of beauty,' he was not bound by perceptible stones; rather, one is crowned from such stones. For instance, Joseph contended regarding temperance. Temperance is a precious stone. These [virtues] crowned him, as well as Susanna and the martyrs. And since virtues follow one another, and he who has one has all, the woven crown is not a single stone. Therefore, 'from a precious stone you placed a crown upon his head.' The 'precious' pertains to that which the precious thing is. We call these stones here, such as pearls and hyacinths and the others, precious, because they are also stones distinct from those. Since, therefore, these great stones are kinds of virtue, behold, these stones are precious and surpass all those appearing to be so in the world.

And that the disciples of the teachers are crowns, Paul taught: 'my joy and crown,' addressing the church that discipled him. 'On that day the Lord of Sabaoth will be the crown of hope.' The material of this crown is the Lord of Sabaoth; for 'the Lord of Sabaoth will be the crown of hope.' And since anyone being there cannot yet have a perfect participation in God, but this will happen when 'God becomes all in all,' becoming a fire perfected in all, in the final desired one; for this reason he called it a crown of hope. For if we are to know Him then, when we see Him as He is, and when we see Him by seeing Him as He is, when we have reached the end, this crown is of hope. It is of end-hope, it is that which we await. 'She sought life from you, and you gave it to him.' We say that the Savior [acts] according to the man—if indeed

title: The Nature of Blessed Life
english: I say 'according to man', do not divide him from the Word—because he is a 'Paraclete' 'towards the Father' (John 14:16). Neither is the Word without the man, nor the man without the Word, but the one joined from both becomes a Paraclete and 'living always to intercede on their behalf' (1 John 2:1) intercedes. Therefore he asks for that life which he wants to be made alive by. And through him the life-giving happens; for he was 'slain in the flesh and made alive in spirit' (Romans 8:11). And the soul of Jesus is not life, but has the living by God measuring and granting it; and all the other souls, as to say each one: 'my soul lives by him'. The soul has a value according to immortality. But 'to live toward God' bears fruit from that which is upon us, just as living again by sin is from that which is upon us.

Length of days into an age and into the age of the age. Again, the length of days we are not able to take up explicitly. But 'into the age' he says 'and into the age of the age'. And these days which are given and become by the sun, are called in this one age only. And it has been said also: 'when will these things be, and what is the sign of your presence and the consummation of the age?' (Matthew 24:3); and: 'until the consummation of this age'. And 'in the days' of the age, if the Scriptures say, they say the days of the age. This one who asked is great and did not send a prayer about a small and indifferent thing, so that even his prayer is remembered, nor about these days which pass by the sun and moon. Otherwise, therefore, these things are to be considered. And it is owed to note that in the Scriptures many times such things fall away and seem as impossible.

'Honor', he says, 'your father and your mother, so that it may go well with you and you may be long-lived on the earth' (Exodus 20:12). But not always the one honoring parents remains for many years in the land. Many younger ones are transferred. For it has been said in the Wisdom of Solomon about such things: 'he was snatched away, not by wickedness, but his understanding changed or deceit deceived his soul' (Wisdom 4:13). And he says that: 'having been perfected in a little while, he filled long ages'. And he says that prudence is great and old age is an uncorrupted life. But if uncorrupted life is old age, it does not consist of days, but of virtue; differently it must be taken.

the days. Therefore, 'he asked you for life' is not so that he himself might live, but so that those for whom he offers the prayer might. Concerning life, we are not speaking of the common kind, but that which is according to virtue. He who has not known sin, nor even done it, nor even held a guile in his heart, did not have a mortality extending toward the blessed life. Therefore, asking for life, he did not ask for himself, but he wants that to be given to them for whom he offers the petition; for he is 'living always to the point of encountering' those who are to have life through him.

Therefore, 'he asked you for life, and you gave it to him.' He says this to God, either the psalmist or the Holy Spirit within him. And it is a great testimony when, having sent up the prayer, he receives the requests. So you gave it to him, 'length of days for ever and ever unto the age of ages.' The saints do not wish at all to have a long-lasting common life in this life. For instance, he says, 'it is better to dissolve and be with Christ' (Phil 1:23). And again: 'Woe, that my sojourn has been lengthened' (Ps 119:18). 'I am a stranger in a land' (Gen 23:4).

He who is 'a stranger and a sojourner' has a longing and a goal to depart from the sojourn, in order to dwell in the appropriate place. Just as the life indicated there is not a common life, which even impious men and irrational animals live, so also 'length of days' does not mean a long-lasting life, but 'length of days,' just as he who honored his parents will be long-lasting and long-lived. And in Deuteronomy it is said: 'This is your life and this is the length of days,' of 'loving the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul' (Deut 6:5). Behold, even the length of days is [that of] one loving Him with all the soul and all the power and all the longing.

Therefore, 'length of days unto the age.' These things can be taken regarding the blessed life in this way: for there is a life which is the same as the knowledge concerning God. When it was being said: 'And this is the eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Him whom you sent, Jesus Christ' (John 17:3), this life is the knowledge concerning the Father and the Son. And again: 'He who believes in me has eternal life' (John 6:47). He who believes in the Savior does not have a common life. The impious are often found to be more long-lasting than the diligent.
